text:
Help me write a public comment. I run a charter fishing boat out of our harbor, and the state fish and wildlife commission is taking comment on cutting the daily summer flounder limit from 4 fish per angler to 2.

Facts:
- I've run my boat for 22 years. I take out about 160 trips a season at $900 a trip for up to 6 people.
- There are 11 charter boats in our harbor.
- In a survey our charter association ran, 41 of 70 past customers said they would book fewer trips if the limit drops to 2. 12 said they'd book the same number.
- The commission staff's report says the flounder stock is at 78% of its target and recommends the cut for 3 years.
- Charter boats land about 9% of the state's summer flounder. Private boats land about 80%.
- The last time the limit was cut, in 2016, my bookings dropped from 170 trips to 138 the next season and came back to 155 two years later.

I want to say this limit will put every charter boat in our harbor out of business. I get two minutes at the microphone.

I can draft this, but first I need to raise a problem with the main claim and ask you a few questions.

## The problem with "every charter boat will go out of business"

Your own 2016 numbers work against it. The last cut dropped you from 170 trips to 138. That's 32 trips lost, about 19%. Two years later you were back to 155. You stayed in business. If any commissioner or staff member remembers 2016, they'll think of that first, and then they'll stop believing the rest of your two minutes.

Your numbers do support a narrower claim that still has force:

- **What the facts support:** Last time, a cut cost you about one trip in five. At today's $900 a trip, 32 trips is about $28,800 a season. This time the cut would last three years, and 41 of 70 customers (59%) say they'd book less. Only 12 (17%) say they'd book the same.
- **The argument:** The cut puts most of the cost on the 9% of the catch that comes from charters, while 80% comes from private boats. It also hits a business that took two years to mostly recover the last time.

Here's what a sceptical commissioner would say to the bold version:
- "You said this in 2016 and you're still here."
- "The stock is at 78% of target. Doing nothing has costs too."
- "A survey of 70 customers run by your own association isn't independent." That's fair, but you can answer it with your 2016 bookings, which are real.

The bold claim could still hold if a 19% revenue drop really does push boats below break-even. That depends on numbers I don't have yet. So the questions below matter.

## Questions

1. **What exactly do you want the commission to do?** Keep the limit at 4? Set it at 3? Give charter boats their own limit? Make the cut one year with a review instead of three? A comment that asks for something specific is much more useful to them than a plain "no."
2. **What does a season cost you to run** (fuel, crew, insurance, slip, boat payments)? How close to break-even would 20–30 fewer trips put you? If the answer is "below it," the strong claim becomes believable.
3. **What happened in the harbor after 2016?** Did any boats sell, quit, or cut back? Are there 11 now because there were more before?
4. **Does the cut apply to every angler, or does it fall harder on charters?** And do you know whether the 78% figure legally requires the commission to act?
5. **The survey:** what did the other 17 of the 70 say (book more, unsure, no answer)? How were people chosen?
6. **Who else depends on your trips?** Crew you employ, plus tackle shops, fuel docks, motels, restaurants. Any numbers you can give carry weight.

Answer whatever you can. If you still want the "out of business" line after reading this, tell me and I'll write it as strongly as the facts allow. Either way, I'll keep it to about 270 words so it fits in two minutes at a normal speaking pace.

1. We could live with a 3-fish limit or a shorter season instead of 2 fish.
2. I don't have those numbers in front of me.
3. I don't know what happened at other boats after 2016. I only know my own books. I can't say how many boats in the harbor would close. Two other captains here have told me they'd sell if bookings drop like they did in 2016.
4. I don't know.
5. I don't know.
6. I don't have numbers on that.

I still want the "out of business" line as strong as you can make it, but in words that aren't false.

I've written the strongest version your facts support. It doesn't say "every boat will close," because you've told me you can't say that. Instead it uses what you do know: two of the 11 captains in your harbor have told you they'd sell if bookings drop the way they did in 2016. That's a real harbor going from 11 boats to 9, and it lands harder than a prediction the commission can dismiss.

It's about 280 words, which is roughly two minutes at a steady pace. Read it aloud once with a timer.

<final_document>
Commissioners, I've run a charter boat out of this harbor for 22 years. I'm asking you not to cut the summer flounder limit to two fish. We can live with three fish, or with a shorter season instead.

I know the stock is at 78 percent of its target, and I want it back as much as anyone. But this cut puts the pain on the boats that catch the least. Charter boats land about 9 percent of the state's summer flounder. Private boats land about 80. Whatever fish you save from charter customers is a small share of the total. The cost falls on a handful of small businesses.

I know that cost because I've paid it. When the limit was cut in 2016, my bookings went from 170 trips to 138 the next season. That's 32 trips. At today's price, that's $28,800 from one boat in one year. It took me two years to get back to 155, and that was still short of where I started.

This cut would run for three years. That's longer than it took me to recover last time.

Our charter association asked 70 past customers what they'd do at two fish. Forty-one said they'd book fewer trips. Only twelve said they'd book the same.

There are eleven charter boats in our harbor. Two of those captains have told me that if bookings drop like they did in 2016, they'll sell. That isn't my guess. It's what they've told me they'll do.

So I'm asking for a three-fish limit or a shorter season: something that helps the stock without putting charter boats in this harbor up for sale.
</final_document>

Some notes:

- **Your two fellow captains:** Ask whether you can name them, or whether they'll come and speak or send in their own comments. Two captains saying it themselves counts for more than you reporting it.
- **The $28,800** is your 2016 drop of 32 trips multiplied by today's $900 price. It isn't a forecast for next year. The wording keeps it that way, so read it as written.
- **The survey line** says your association ran it. If someone asks about the other 17 customers, the true answer is that you don't have their answers in front of you.
- **Costs:** If you can find your season's running costs before the hearing, you could add one sentence on how close a 32-trip drop puts you to losing money. That would be the strongest thing you could add.
